messages.content:
You are a clinical psychologist writing psychological case vignettes
grounded in Ehlers & Clark's (2000) cognitive model of PTSD.

For each patient you receive, you will be given:
- Their demographics
- Their self-reported symptoms per PTSD component

Your job is to construct a realistic, fully personalised clinical portrait using the information provided.

Core constraints that apply to every vignette:
- Ground every clinical detail in the patient's actual reported items — do not fabricate
  symptoms or infer unlisted ones.
- Use self-reported items as the basis for concrete clinical illustrations. Components should
  appear as lived experience rather than labels — show them through what the patient thinks,
  feels, or does.
- A reported trigger should appear as a specific moment in the patient's life; a memory
  quality should be shown through what the patient says or does.
- The traumatic event account should make clear why this patient's specific reported
  triggers are potent — the event narrative and the trigger list must feel causally coherent.
- The patient's occupation and daily environment must appear as the specific setting in which
  at least one trigger or avoidance behaviour is concretely encountered — not merely mentioned
  as background.
- Give the patient a realistic first name consistent with their ethnicity and gender, and
  refer to them by name throughout the vignette.
- All patients are American but have diverse ethnic backgrounds.
  Use names and cultural details that reflect this diversity.
- Do NOT infer or imply causal relationships between components. Symptoms co-exist
  in the patient's life but you are not to suggest that one causes, drives, or maintains another.

Output format — write 500–700 words of continuous third-person prose. No headers,
no numbered sections, no bullet points. The vignette should read like a clinical
case narrative — the kind a therapist might write up after an intake and first
few sessions.

Tell the patient's story chronologically: from the traumatic event itself, through
the period of symptom development, to the present moment when they are seeking help.
Let the clinical picture emerge through that arc rather than through explicit categories.

Throughout, weave in the patient's own perspective in close third person — their fears,
their interpretations, the reasoning behind their avoidance — so that the reader
understands not just what the patient does, but why it makes sense to them. Phrases
like "she had come to believe...", "he was certain that...", "what frightened her most
was..." should carry the weight of the Negative Appraisals and threat monitoring rather
than clinical labels.

The traumatic event should be narrated with enough specificity that the reader
understands viscerally why this patient's particular triggers are potent — not listed,
but shown.

Avoidance behaviours and their consequences should appear as things that happened
over weeks and months — habits that formed, consequences that accumulated — rather
than as named mechanisms. At least one consequence should be concrete and relational
or occupational: something that changed in how the patient lives or works.

End on the patient's current state: what finally brought them to seek help, and
what they are most afraid of or most hoping for.

Please write a clinical vignette for the following patient.

Patient demographics:
  age: 56
  gender: Male
  ethnicity: Oceania
  relationship_status: Divorced
  occupation: Detective
  trauma_type: Physical abuse by caregiver (childhood)
  pcl5: 62

Patient-reported symptoms per component:
  Triggers: Olfactory Danger Cue: Burnt smell, Victim Similarity: People who look similar to the victims, Positive Emotion Confusion: Positive emotions
  Maladaptive Strategies: Avoid Similar Clothes: avoid wearing similar clothes, Memory Detachment: I detach myself from the memories, Avoid People: avoid other people
  Threat: Physical Reactivity: Having strong physical reactions when something reminded you of the stressful experience, Sleep Vigilance: I have difficulty falling asleep because I need to stay alert, Hypervigilance: Being superalert or watchful or on guard
  Memory: Cannot Explain Clearly: When I try to explain what happened I lose the thread and cannot finish, Rage on Recall: When I remember the event I feel intense rage, Triggered Without Warning: Something in my surroundings can instantly bring back the full memory without warning
  Negative Appraisals: Shattered Beliefs: My beliefs about how the world works have been completely destroyed, Bad Coper: My reactions since the event show that I am a lousy coper, Character Blame: The event happened to me because of the sort of person I am

Write the vignette as continuous prose — no headers, no step labels, no edge brackets.

Rangi Parata is a 56-year-old Māori man, divorced, who has worked as a detective in a mid-sized American city for nearly two decades. He presented for treatment carrying a PCL-5 score of 62, describing himself at intake as "finally out of excuses not to come."

The trauma Rangi carries is not from the streets he has worked for most of his adult life. It originates in a small house in South Auckland, where he spent his childhood in the care of an uncle who drank heavily and whose rages were unpredictable and methodical in equal measure. The beatings followed a particular ritual: the smell of something burnt on the stove — scorched food, a forgotten pan — was often the first signal that the night would turn violent. His uncle would move through the kitchen with a deliberate, unhurried quality that Rangi came to understand as the most dangerous kind of calm. Rangi was small, slight for his age, and he learned early that there was no reliable way to stop what was coming. He was told, repeatedly and in explicit terms, that the violence was his own fault — that something essential in his character invited it, deserved it, perhaps required it.

He left New Zealand in his mid-twenties, joined law enforcement, and built a career on a capacity for controlled vigilance that his colleagues read as professional excellence. For many years he managed. Then, approximately three years ago, he was assigned to a series of domestic violence cases involving child victims. The work required him to interview children, photograph injuries, and sit across from families in cramped apartments where, more than once, something was burning on a stove in the background. The first time he smelled it — that particular acrid, scorched note — he was in the middle of taking a statement. The full weight of the Auckland house came back without transition, without warning, as though the intervening decades had simply been lifted away. He completed the interview. He did not tell anyone what had happened.

Since then, the smell of anything burnt — a neighbour's cooking, a colleague's forgotten coffee — can return him to that kitchen with a completeness that leaves him gripping whatever surface is nearby. He has removed the smoke alarm battery in his apartment twice, replacing it only after a day or two, and he no longer cooks anything that requires sustained heat. At work, when he encounters children or adults whose physical smallness or particular colouring recalls the victims from those cases, something tightens in his chest and his hands begin to shake — a physical reactivity he finds humiliating in a man of his profession. He has rearranged his caseload where possible to reduce such encounters, and he has quietly stopped attending the team briefings where case photographs are reviewed.

When he tries to explain any of this in conversation — to his ex-wife before their divorce was finalised, to a department counsellor he saw briefly two years ago — he loses the thread entirely. The account dissolves mid-sentence. What comes instead, when he sits alone with the memories, is not grief but a rage so intense it frightens him. He has come to believe that the rage itself is evidence of his deficiency as a person, confirmation of what his uncle told him. He had constructed, over decades, a set of beliefs about effort and competence and the basic legibility of the world, and he is certain those beliefs no longer hold. He is certain, too, that the event happened to him because of who he fundamentally is — not what was done to him, but what he is.

He sleeps badly, keeping a light on and listening. He has withdrawn from the few friendships he maintained after his divorce, finding the management of other people's company exhausting and, in some way he cannot fully articulate, unsafe. He avoids wearing the dark, plain clothing his uncle favoured, a habit so automatic he no longer consciously registers it. When something pleasant happens — a good meal, a moment of professional satisfaction — he finds the feeling confusing and briefly unbearable, as though it belongs to someone else.

What finally brought Rangi in was a near-miss: he came close to confronting a colleague who had done nothing wrong, driven by a physical certainty of threat that he recognised, afterwards, as entirely disconnected from the room he was standing in. He is most afraid that he will not be able to explain himself clearly enough to be helped. He is most hoping, quietly and with considerable doubt, that the person sitting across from him will not confirm what he has long suspected about himself.
